title: Training labels as tensors (batch)
text:
Training labels as tensors (batch)
• Nmax: the maximum number of objects in one image after batching — take the
max number of boxes over images in the batch, then pad images with fewer
boxes to the same length Nmax.
• loc gt ∈RB×Nmax×4: GT coordinates for each slot in the tensor.
• Typical format (YOLO / Ultralytics label file): each row is
(cx, cy, w, h), normalized by image width and height (each value ∈[0, 1]):
box center and relative size.
• Some pipelines use normalized (x1, y1, x2, y2) or absolute pixel coordinates
— the important point is to be consistent with the assignment step and
the loss function; later slides in this deck use cell anchors / offsets on the
feature map after GT boxes already exist in image coordinates.
• cls gt ∈RB×Nmax×1 (or ZB×Nmax): class index 0, . . . , Nc −1 for each box slot
(padded slots may receive dummy values and are removed by mask).
• mask ∈RB×Nmax×1 (usually binary or {0, 1}): 1 = valid GT slot, 0 = padding
slot after aligning to Nmax — used to avoid computing loss / assigning labels on
fake slots.

title: Overall Architecture - Neck
text:
Overall Architecture - Neck
• Low-level features preserve object details, but lack large-context
information.
• High-level features preserve large-context information, but lack fine
object details.
• The responsibility of the Neck is to fuse multi-scale features (FPN/PAN)
to improve detection of small/medium/large objects.
• FPN (Feature Pyramid Network): propagates semantic information
from deep layers to shallow layers through upsample + merge.
• PAN (Path Aggregation Network): propagates positional/detail
information from shallow layers back to deep layers through downsample +
merge.
• Result: each feature level has both local details and strong context.

title: Overall Architecture - NMS
text:
Overall Architecture - NMS
Non-Maximum Suppression (NMS)
• Role: used only during inference after training; it is not learned directly
through the loss.
• Purpose: reduce the list of overlapping boxes — keep strong predictions
and remove duplicates for the same object.
• Typical procedure: per class, sort boxes by confidence; repeatedly take
the top box and remove remaining boxes whose IoU overlap is ≥the
threshold (greedy non-maximum suppression).
• Usually applied after conf filtering; variants exist (multiclass-NMS,
soft-NMS, etc.), but the core idea remains the same.

Loss in YOLO — Overview
• After the assignment step {mik}, the loss is a weighted sum following one-stage
training:
L = wboxLbox + wclsLcls + wdflLdfl.
• Lbox, Ldfl: computed only on pairs (i, k) with mik = 1 (and normalized by the
number of samples / batch).
• Lcls: multi-label BCE over all Na positions — positive cells are one-hot
according to ck, while background cells are zero vectors.
Different from some query-based detectors
No Hungarian matching is needed: local assignment based on tik and top-r ⇒
essentially one-to-many, unlike global one-to-one matching.

• The previous slides described the general architecture of one-stage YOLO detectors:
Image →Backbone →Neck →Head →NMS
• In the Ultralytics YAML configuration:
• the backbone: section describes the main feature extraction layers;
• the head: section usually includes both the FPN/PAN Neck and the
final Detect layer.
• Therefore, when reading YAML, we should conceptually separate:
head:
in YAML ≈Neck + Detection Head
• YOLOv8 and YOLO11 share the same detection-head philosophy: anchor-free, DFL
for box regression, and sigmoid/BCE for classification. The main differences lie in the
feature processing blocks in the backbone and neck.
Correct way to read
Do not read YAML only by the names backbone/head; instead, map it back to the three
academic modules: Backbone – Neck – Head.

YOLOv8 — Backbone
• The YOLOv8 backbone uses the following main blocks:
Conv,
C2f,
SPPF
• Conv: reduces spatial resolution and increases the number of feature channels.
• C2f: a CSP-style block that improves representation power while keeping
computational cost reasonable.
• SPPF: aggregates context at deep layers using fast pooling.
Backbone feature levels
P3 : stride 8,
P4 : stride 16,

• Preprocessing: image →resize/letterbox to imgsz, and normalize

• Filtering: remove predictions whose conf is below the threshold; limit
the maximum number of candidates (max det) if configured.
• Post-processing: class-wise NMS (next slide); map coordinates back to
the original image when letterbox was used.

title: DETR: What are the inference steps?
text:
DETR: What are the inference steps?
(1) Image preprocessing: resize/normalize according to the model configuration.
(2) Backbone + Encoder: extract image features and encode global context.
(3) Decoder with queries: let Nq object queries attend to the image memory to
create object-wise embeddings.
(4) Prediction head: each query produces class logits (including no-object) and
a normalized box.
(5) Prediction filtering: remove low-score/no-object queries, and keep top-k by
score.
(6) Coordinate post-processing: convert boxes from normalized coordinates back
to the original image size (undo resize/padding if needed).
Note
DETR inference usually does not need YOLO-style NMS because the one-to-one
mechanism is learned during training.

title: Summary: Inference and Evaluation
text:
Summary: Inference and Evaluation
• Inference pipeline:
Image →Forward →Decode boxes →Confidence filter →NMS →Final detections
• NMS is used to remove strongly duplicated boxes.
• Detection evaluation is based on:
• IoU;
• TP / FP / FN;
• Precision / Recall;
• AP / mAP.
• mAP is meaningful only when data, labels, splits, and the evaluation pipeline
are properly controlled.

What to Remember After This Lecture
• Do not learn YOLO only by version names; learn it through the structure:
data →feature pyramid →head →decode →evaluation
• When reading YOLO source code:
• read the YAML file to understand the model graph;
• read block.py to understand backbone/neck blocks;
• read head.py to understand the Detect head;
• read loss/eval code to understand training and mAP computation.
• The final goal: not only to use YOLO, but to modify YOLO, analyze YOLO,
and design new detectors.
